newsitem.title: USA: Fed's Greenspan sees less govt regulation ahead.
newsitem.headline: Fed's Greenspan sees less govt regulation ahead.

text.p: Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan said on Saturday that he foresaw a bright future where much unwieldy government regulation was swept away by new technology.

In a speech prepared for delivery to the Association of Private Enterprise Education in nearby Arlington, Va., the central bank chief said the impact of computer technology already was evident in fields like finance, communications and transportation.

"As we move into a new century, the market-stabilizing private regulatory forces should gradually displace many cumbersome, increasingly ineffective government structures," he said in remarks that were released in advance of delivery.
Regulatory restraints against interstate banking and against combinations of investment and commercial banking already are being pushed aside by the pressure of technological change, Greenspan said.
Big banking conglomerates now offer many more services than merely deposit-taking and loans, taking advantage of powerful computers to expand their competitive reach.
"...The rapidly changing technology that is rendering much government bank regulation irrelevant also bids fair to undercut regulatory efforts in a much wider segment of our economy," Greenspan said.
He said the reason was that regulation was inherently conservative and sought to preserve the staus quo while the creation of wealth necessarily requires risk-taking.
"With technological change clearly accelerating, existing regulatory structures are being bypassed, freeing market forces to enhance wealth creation and economic growth," Greenspan said.
The pace of computer-driven change might be unsettling for many Americans, the Fed chief said, but it was not a threat.
"Fortunately, our children appear to thrive on it," said Greenspan. "The future accordingly looks bright."
